readerTitle: Same price, less inside: the quiet price rise
caseNote: 일상 장면 (포장 과자) + 가상 사례 (가사 청소 서비스, 마케팅 대행사) + 실제 연구 (시카고 아이스크림 시장)
insight: 슈링크플레이션은 가격을 그대로 둔 '조용한 가격 인상'이다. 단위당 가격으로 다시 계산하면 생각보다 큰 인상인 경우가 많고, 고객이 알아차리는 순간 신뢰 비용을 치른다. 줄이려면 고객이 덜 쓰는 것을 공개적으로 줄인다.
misconception: 가격표 숫자만 그대로면 고객은 가격이 오른 것으로 느끼지 않고, 들키지 않으면 손해도 없다.

sources.text: Çakır, M. & Balagtas, J. V. (2014). Consumer Response to Package Downsizing: Evidence from the Chicago Ice Cream Market. Journal of Retailing, 90(1).
청소 서비스와 마케팅 대행사 사례의 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Çakır & Balagtas(2014) 연구의 결론(소비자가 같은 크기의 가격 인상보다 포장 축소에 덜 민감하게 반응한다)을 원문으로 다시 확인하세요. 카드에는 구체 수치 없이 방향만 적었습니다.
청소 서비스 계산: $90 ÷ 3시간 = 시간당 $30, $90 ÷ 2.5시간 = 시간당 $36. 36 ÷ 30 = 1.2, 즉 시간당 20% 인상. 비용 상승 가정은 10%.
일부 국가와 유통사가 용량이 줄어든 상품에 표시를 붙이기 시작했다는 내용은 법률 조언이 되지 않도록 카드에 넣지 않았습니다.

cards.title: The price didn't change. The bag did.
body: You buy the same bag of crisps you always buy. Same price, same colors, same shelf. But it feels lighter, and there's more air when you open it.
You check the label. A little less inside than last time. Nobody raised the price. Or did they?

image.label: Two snack bags, same price tag, one slightly smaller
image.brief: 마트 진열대에 똑같은 디자인의 과자 봉지 두 개. 가격표는 둘 다 같고, 오른쪽 봉지만 살짝 작고 안의 내용물이 적게 보이는 단면 표시. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Your costs are up 10%.
body: You run a home cleaning service. A standard visit is 3 hours for $90. Wages and supplies have risen about 10% this year, and your margins are thin.

options.text: Raise the visit price by 10%, with a clear note to clients
options.feedback: Honest and simple, and it covers your costs. Some price-sensitive clients may leave, and you haven't checked whether there's a cheaper fix clients would prefer.

options.text: Keep $90, but quietly shorten visits to 2.5 hours
options.feedback: No awkward price conversation today. But regular clients notice when the cleaner leaves early, and the hidden cut is bigger than you think. Next card shows why.

options.text: Keep $90, drop the task clients rarely want (like inside the oven), tell them, and offer it as an add-on
options.feedback: You save time where clients care least, and nobody discovers a cut they weren't told about. The work is knowing what they value.

cards.title: Price it per hour.
body: Your costs rose 10%. The quiet cut raised your real price **20%**: twice what you needed, and hidden.

breakdown.label: Real price rise
breakdown.detail: What clients pay for each hour

cards.title: Shrinkflation
body: **Shrinkflation** means giving customers less for the same price: a smaller pack, a shorter visit, fewer hours. It's a price increase that the price tag doesn't show.

Its cousin is cutting quality instead of quantity, like cheaper ingredients or slower service. The test is the same for both: divide the price by what the customer actually gets. That's the real price.

image.label: Price tag stays fixed while the product behind it shrinks
image.brief: 가격표 하나가 고정되어 있고, 그 뒤의 상자가 세 단계로 점점 작아지는 그림. 아래에 "Price per unit" 막대가 점점 높아짐. 로고 없음.

cards.title: People watch the price, not the size.
body: The price is one big number. The quantity is small print, and comparing per unit takes effort. So a smaller size often slips past.
A study of the Chicago ice cream market by Çakır and Balagtas (2014) found that shoppers reacted less to package downsizing than to a price rise of similar size.
That's the appeal for sellers. It's also why customers feel tricked when they finally notice.

cards.title: Services shrink too.
body: A restaurant serves smaller portions. A plumber's call-out fee now covers 30 minutes instead of an hour. A consultancy's monthly fee buys fewer meetings. A hotel stops daily room cleaning but keeps the rate.
In each case the price stays put while the **unit** of what you sell gets smaller.
cards.softwareNote: In software it looks like lower usage limits, fewer seats or a feature moved to a pricier tier, all on the same plan price. Users spot it fast, because they hit the new limit in the middle of their work.

cards.title: Hidden cuts get found.
body: Regular customers notice changes in what they use every week. When they do, the story isn't "prices went up". It's "they hoped I wouldn't notice". That can hurt trust more than an open price rise.

Shrinking isn't always wrong. Cutting what customers barely use can be a fair trade. The difference is whether you choose the cut carefully and say it out loud. And if a contract promises a quantity, cutting it isn't shrinkflation. It's breaking the deal.

cards.title: Now it's a marketing agency.
body: Clients pay you $4,000 a month for 20 hours of work. Your staff costs are up about 10%. Your time logs show most clients use only about 15 of their 20 hours.

options.feedback: That's a hidden 25% rise per hour. The first client who checks the report will ask why, and you'll be explaining a secret instead of a price.

options.text: Keep 20 hours and raise the fee to $4,400, with notice
options.feedback: Open and fair, and it covers your costs. But most clients pay more for hours they don't use, which invites them to shop around.

options.text: Offer a 16-hour plan at $4,000 and a 20-hour plan at $4,400, and explain why
options.feedback: Clients who use 15 hours lose nothing they value, and heavy users keep their hours at a clear price. You shrink the offer in the open.

cards.title: Less for the same price is still a price rise.
body: Always divide the price by what customers get. If you must shrink, cut what they value least and tell them.
**Try it today:** pick one product or service. Write its price per unit (per gram, per hour, per visit) now and a year ago. Did it rise more than you thought?
